stories.headline: Nvidia faces FBI scrutiny, a shareholder suit and calls in Congress for probes over CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy
stories.summary: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. President Trump said the FBI is looking into it, Nvidia hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to run an internal investigation, shareholders sued, and lawmakers from both parties called for inquiries. Nvidia shares fell sharply on Monday and Tuesday and were reported up about 5% on Wednesday as investors look toward the company's earnings.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the stock market, so its swings move the retirement and index funds many people hold, and the scandal is adding momentum to proposed limits on selling U.S. AI chips abroad.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most artificial-intelligence systems, and Jensen Huang is its co-founder and chief executive. Huang has been one of the most prominent voices urging Washington to ease export controls on selling advanced chips to China. Over the weekend he acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former Shanghai banker turned tech executive at Megaspeed, a company under U.S. investigation over alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China, which it denies. Nvidia's board opened an investigation and said it still has confidence in Huang, while Trump has publicly defended him.

facts.text: Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence has identified as suspected of spying for China, according to reporting by CBS, the BBC and CNBC.
Alice Huang is a Chinese banker turned tech executive who worked at Megaspeed, according to an AP profile.
Megaspeed is under U.S. investigation over alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China, which it denies, DW reported.
Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, and that Huang told him he had no idea she was a spy.

Nvidia's board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would oversee an investigation, and that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
Trump has publicly defended Huang, calling him an "honorable guy."
Nvidia hired Wachtell Lipton to lead the internal inquiry, headed by partner Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney in Manhattan.
Nvidia and Huang face a shareholder lawsuit filed in California alleging investors were misled about the affair.
Republicans and Democrats have both called for investigations into whether national security was compromised, but differ on whether the Trump administration is at fault, The Hill reported.
The senior Republican on the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to resign, Reuters reported.
Lawmakers are pushing new rules on chip sales to China, and the scandal has added momentum to three bills that would restrict chip exports.
A blacklisted Chinese university linked to the military bought Nvidia H200 chips despite U.S. export rules, according to procurement records reported by Reuters.
Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, erasing roughly $200 billion in market value, CBS reported.

The stock was down 5.9% at $168.12 on Tuesday, with nearly $450 billion lost over two days, the New York Post reported, and Microsoft passed Nvidia in market value for the first time since June 2025, per Reuters.
Nvidia shares were up about 5% on Wednesday as investors weighed whether the affair will affect the business ahead of earnings, CNBC reported.
Major Nvidia investors publicly backed Huang while privately expressing disappointment, Axios reported.

disputed.topic: What the administration knew before the affair became public

positions.claim: Trump has said Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy, and the Times describes the president as denying he had been told.

The New York Times reports Trump was reminded of the intelligence before Huang boarded Air Force One for Beijing, and Axios reports Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a classified memo about the relationship.

stories.headline: Hotter-than-expected October inflation raises bets on a December Fed rate hike
stories.summary: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, less than in September but more than economists expected, with food, energy and housing costs all rising. Several Federal Reserve officials signaled support for raising interest rates again, traders priced in a December hike, short-term Treasury yields jumped and the dollar rose. U.S. stocks slipped on Tuesday; the bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher interest rates make mortgages, car loans and credit-card balances more expensive, while inflation running near 4% means paychecks buy less.
stories.background: The Consumer Price Index, published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, tracks what households pay for a basket of goods and services. Prices have been pushed up this year in part by an energy shock tied to the U.S.-Iran war. The Federal Reserve fights inflation by raising its benchmark interest rate, which makes borrowing costlier and cools spending. Its next rate decision is at the Dec. 9 meeting, and officials including Christopher Waller have been signaling more hikes.

facts.text: The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above forecasts.
The monthly increase was smaller than September's, but economists called it still uncomfortably high, CNBC reported.
Shelter, food and energy costs drove the increase, though gasoline prices dipped during the month.
Axios reported that October was the third straight month of hotter-than-expected inflation.
PBS NewsHour said the country appears headed for annual inflation of about 4% this year.
Fed official Christopher Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December, Reuters reported.
Fed official Lorie Logan called for two more hikes, possibly in quick succession, and Fed official Anna Paulson called for gradual hikes, according to Reuters.
Traders are betting on near-certain odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's Dec. 9 meeting, the New York Post reported.
Two-year Treasury yields jumped the most since 2024 after the report, and the dollar rose to a four-week high.
U.S. stocks slipped on Tuesday following the report.
The Treasury market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.

stories.headline: Gas falls below $4 as oil slides on Trump's Iran comments, then edges back up
stories.summary: Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel, its lowest since late August, after President Trump said the war with Iran is "effectively over" and pulled back from threats of further strikes. The national average price of gasoline dropped to $3.98, the first time below $4 since July, according to AAA. Oil rose again on Wednesday after a two-day decline as traders weighed uncertainty over U.S.-Iran talks.
stories.why_it_matters: Cheaper gasoline gives drivers some relief, though overall living costs remain high and oil prices are still swinging on news from the Iran conflict.
stories.background: Oil prices surged after the U.S. attack on Iran, because the Persian Gulf is a major route for the world's crude. Brent, the global benchmark, traded around $113 a barrel in late October. Prices have fallen in November as Trump signaled restraint, which also helped global stocks recover from the prior week's sell-off. Gasoline prices follow crude with a lag.

facts.text: Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel, the lowest since late August, after Trump said the Iran war is effectively over.
The global benchmark is down more than $20 a barrel since late October, when it traded around $113, the New York Times reported.
Falling crude helped support a recovery in global stocks from the prior week's sell-off, the Financial Times reported.
The national average gasoline price fell to $3.98 a gallon, the first time below $4 since July, according to AAA.
Oil rose on Wednesday after a two-day decline as traders weighed mixed signals on ending the Iran war.
Reuters reported oil rose about 1% after Iran said no nuclear material would leave the country.

stories.headline: Anthropic targets a trillion-dollar-plus valuation for its IPO, with reports it may go higher
stories.summary: AI company Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, is seeking a valuation of roughly $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion in a stock market listing expected next week, according to multiple reports. The Financial Times reported that bankers are preparing to raise the target to $1.5 trillion or more after strong investor demand, and Anthropic opened a retail offering in Australia on Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: It would be one of the largest stock listings ever, and investors are treating it as a test of whether the AI boom that has driven stock indexes can continue.
stories.background: Anthropic is an artificial-intelligence company that develops the Claude family of AI models. It filed to go public in the fall, and an amended filing this month added third-quarter results showing revenue of about $17 billion for the quarter. Earlier reports had it aiming for about $2 trillion before investors cooled on AI stocks. Large tech companies including Nvidia and TSMC are investing alongside the listing. (Note: this brief is produced with Claude, an Anthropic product.)

facts.text: Anthropic is seeking a valuation of about $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion in its IPO.
Anthropic plans to raise as much as $64 billion, the Financial Times reported.
Anthropic had been reported to be aiming for a $2 trillion valuation before investors cooled on AI, the Guardian reported.
Seven co-founders' stakes are worth about $18 billion each at the IPO price; each plans to sell about $250 million in shares and they keep voting control, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Nvidia plans to invest $10 billion alongside the IPO, the New York Times reported, and TSMC earmarked up to $1 billion for Anthropic and OpenAI shares.
Anthropic opened a retail IPO offering to individual investors in Australia on Wednesday.
Traders in perpetual futures are betting the shares will rise after the listing, CNBC reported.
Anthropic's amended filing showed third-quarter revenue of $17.0 billion and an operating loss of $567 million.

stories.headline: CoreWeave results lift AI stocks after a rough stretch
stories.summary: Shares of AI cloud provider CoreWeave rose about 11% after it beat revenue expectations and raised its outlook, easing worries about an AI slowdown. U.S. stock futures and European chip stocks rose on Wednesday, with Nasdaq futures leading, as investors returned to the AI trade after Tuesday's inflation-driven dip.
stories.why_it_matters: AI-related companies make up a large share of U.S. stock indexes, so investor confidence in the AI boom affects the value of many retirement accounts; coverage came mainly from center and left-leaning financial outlets.
stories.background: CoreWeave is one of the so-called neoclouds, companies that rent out large banks of Nvidia chips for AI work. These firms borrow heavily to build data centers, and investors this month questioned whether AI demand can sustain that spending. The Nasdaq is down more than 8% over the past month, and investors have been shifting into defensive sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare. CoreWeave's results were watched as a sign of AI demand.

facts.text: CoreWeave shares rose about 11% after the company raised its outlook.
CoreWeave beat third-quarter revenue expectations and announced $9 billion in planned customer prepayments, MarketWatch reported.
CoreWeave is targeting profitability in 2028, Reuters reported.

European chip stocks climbed and European indexes neared a record high.
Investors have been moving into defensive sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare amid worries about tech earnings.
